titleEn: The Song of the Cid — Búcar's message; Fernando's cowardice; the bishop opens the battle (tiradas 115–117, lines 2338–2402)
part: Tiradas 115–117 · Búcar's message; Fernando's cowardice; the bishop opens the battle (lines 2338–2402)

sentences.t: “aun vea el ora que vos meresca dos tanto.”
sentences.l: “may-I-yet see the hour that from-you I-may-earn two so-much.”
sentences.i: “May I yet live to see the hour when I can repay you twice over.”
sentences.n: Tirada 115 (assonance á-o) — Búcar's message; the Christians' charge; the Infante Fernando's cowardice; Per Vermudoz's generosity (Pidal: Mensaje de Búcar.—Espolonada de los cristianos. Cobardía del infante Fernando (Laguna del manuscrito, 50 versos que se suplen con el texto de la Crónica de Veinte Reyes). — Generosidad de Pedro Vermúdez). The line-ends run tanto, amos, Ferrando, vasallos, alto: stressed á, then o. Before this line a folio of the manuscript is lost, about fifty lines by Pidal's reckoning, and he fills the gap with italic prose from the Crónica de Veinte Reyes, which is not included here. In outline it tells how Búcar sent to bid the Çid leave Valencia and go in peace, or pay for all he had done there, and the Çid sent back word that within three days he would give Búcar what he asked; how the next day the Çid armed all his men and went out against the Moors, and the Infantes asked him for the vanguard (la delantera; Pidal's note: la delantera, esto es, las heridas primeras; comp. 3317 — 'that is, the first blows'); how Fernando rode out to strike a Moor called Aladraf, and when the Moor came at him turned his rein and fled in fear, not daring even to wait for him; and how Per Vermudoz, riding near, fought the Moor and killed him, took the Moor's horse, rode after the fleeing Infante, and told him to take it and tell everyone he had killed its owner, promising to bear him out. The prose ends with Fernando beginning his thanks; this line, the first that survives, completes his reply. aun, 'yet'; vea, present subjunctive of veer, 'may I see', a wish. meresca, present subjunctive of merecer, 'deserve, earn'; dos tanto, 'twice as much'. Pidal's note: 'ojalá os lo pueda pagar con creces'; literalmente, vos meresca dos tanto, 'merezca de vos el doble' — 'would that I could repay you with interest'; literally 'may I earn from you the double'. He adds that the English hispanophile J. H. Frère, ambassador in Madrid, not understanding the phrase, proposed the correction que vos merescades tanto to the Marqués de la Romana, and later gave a messenger the corrected line as his only credential to Romana, who recognised it as coming from Frère.

sentences.t:
En una conpaña tornados son amos.
Assi lo otorga don Pero qu[o]mo se alaba Ferrando.
sentences.l:
In one company turned are both.
So it confirms don Pero a[s] himself boasts Ferrando.
sentences.i: The two rode back together to the company, and Don Pero bears out every word of Fernando's boasting.
sentences.n: tornados son, 'they have turned back', ser + participle with a verb of motion; amos, 'both', the Infante and Per Vermudoz (don Pero). otorga, 'confirms, grants', present among pasts (the epic tense-mixing). qu[o]mo = commo, 'as', the o Pidal's restoration. se alaba, 'boasts' (alabarse). Per Vermudoz keeps the bargain the lost prose described: Fernando claims the dead Moor and Don Pero swears to it.

sentences.i: My Çid was pleased, and so were all his vassals: “If God wills it, and the Father on high, both my sons-in-law will yet prove good men in the field.”
sentences.n: Plogo, 'it pleased', strong preterite of plazer; the word Çid is Pidal's restoration. The speaker of the next two lines is not named; they read most naturally as the Çid's. Pidal's note: Para Dios e el Padre, comp. v. 300. quisiere, future subjunctive, 'shall wish'. los mios yernos, article + possessive, 'my sons-in-law'. en ca[n]po = en campo, 'in the field, in battle'; Pidal prints the n in italics, though the establishing run marks this italic as one of its least certain readings.

sentences.t:
Esto van diziendo e las yentes se allegando,
en la ueste de los moros los atamores sonando;
a maravilla lo avien muchos dessos cristianos,
ca nunca lo vieran, ca nuevos son llegados.
sentences.l:
This they-go saying and the people themselves gathering,
in the host of the Moors the drums sounding;
at marvel it held many of-those Christians,
for never it they-had-seen, for new are arrived.
sentences.i: While they were saying this, and the men were gathering, the drums were sounding in the Moors' army; many of those Christians held it a marvel, for they had never seen such a thing, being newly come.
sentences.n: van diziendo, ir + gerund, 'they go on saying'; then two loose gerunds, se allegando, 'gathering', and sonando, 'sounding', each with its own subject. ueste = hueste, 'army, host', spelt without h. atamores, 'drums' (from Arabic). Pidal's note to v. 2347: Los tambores desconocidos de los cristianos, p. 107 — 'the drums unknown to the Christians'. a maravilla lo avien, aver a maravilla, 'to hold for a marvel'. dessos = de essos, 'of those'. vieran, the old -ra form as a pluperfect indicative, 'they had seen'. nuevos son llegados, 'they have come new', newly arrived in Valencia.

sentences.t:
Mas se maravillan entre Dí[a]go e Ferrando,
por la su voluntad non serien allí llegados.
sentences.l:
Most themselves marvel between Dí[a]go and Ferrando,
by the their will not they-would-be there arrived.
sentences.i: Most amazed of all were Diego and Fernando: had it been left to them, they would never have come there.
sentences.n: Mas = más, 'more, most'. Pidal's note: entre, v. 191: entre X e Y, 'X and Y together, both'. Dí[a]go, the a Pidal's. por la su voluntad, article + possessive, 'by their own will'. serien … llegados, conditional of seer with the participle, 'they would have arrived'.

sentences.t:
Oíd lo que fabló el que en buen ora nasco:
“¡Ala, Per Vermu[doz], el mio sobrino caro!
sentences.l:
Hear what spoke he who in good hour was-born:
“Ho, Per Vermu[doz], the my nephew dear!
sentences.i: Hear what he said, he who was born in a good hour: “Ho there, Per Vermudoz, my dear nephew!
sentences.n: Oíd, 'hear!', the singer to his audience. fabló = habló (initial f-). el que en buen ora nasco, the Çid's standing title; nasco, strong preterite of naçer. Pidal's note: Ala, '¡ola!'. Recuérdense los versos 2169 y 2177, en que Pero Vermúdez se encarga de los infantes juntamente con Muño Gustioz — 'hey!'; 'remember vv. 2169 and 2177, where Pero Vermúdez takes charge of the Infantes together with Muño Gustioz'. Vermu[doz], the doz Pidal's. el mio sobrino, article + possessive again.

sentences.t:
cúriesme a Dí[da]go e cúriesme a Fernando
mios yernos amos a dos, la cosa que mucho amo,
ca los moros, con Dios, non fincarán en canpo.”
sentences.l:
guard-me Dí[da]go and guard-me Fernando
my sons-in-law both two, the thing that much I-love,
for the Moors, with God, not will-remain in field.”
sentences.i: Look after Diego for me, and look after Fernando, both my sons-in-law, whom I love dearly; for the Moors, God willing, will not hold the field.”
sentences.n: cúriesme, present subjunctive 2nd singular of curiar, 'guard, take care of', used as a command, with me as an ethic dative: 'guard Diego for me'. The Çid speaks to his nephew with the familiar singular (tú), where elsewhere the poem's speakers use vos. Dí[da]go, the da Pidal's. amos a dos, 'both the two'. la cosa que mucho amo, 'the thing I love much', in apposition to the sons-in-law. con Dios, 'with God', God willing. non fincarán en canpo, 'will not remain in the field': they will be driven off it. Tirada 115 ends here.

sentences.i: “I tell you, Çid, in all charity: today the Infantes will not have me for their tutor. Let whoever wants look after them; I care little for them.
sentences.n: Tirada 116 (assonance á, often á-e) — Per Vermudoz washes his hands of the Infantes; Minaya and Don Jerome ask for the first place in the battle (Pidal: Pedro Vermúdez se desentiende de los infantes.—Minaya y don Jerónimo piden el primer puesto en la batalla). The line-ends run caridad, abrán, incal, delant, huviar, Fáñez, leal[e], fera[ve]: stressed á, and from v. 2361b on, several end in -e, a good number of them restored by Pidal (see below). Pidal's dash marks a change of speaker: Per Vermudoz answers. por toda caridad, 'by all charity', an earnest plea. Pidal's note: amo, 'ayo' que cuida a un joven que hace sus primeras armas — 'a tutor who looks after a young man bearing his first arms'. abrán, future of aver, 'will have'. cúrielos = curie + los, present subjunctive 3rd singular, 'let (him) guard them'; qui quier, 'whoever will' (qui 'who', quier, cut-down quiere). Pidal's note: 'pues de ellos poco me importa', v. 230: m' incal = me incal, 'it matters to me', incal, cut-down present of incaler, printed with a space after the apostrophe.

sentences.i: I and my men want to strike them in the front; you and yours, hold firm at the rear; if there is need, you can come to my help.”
sentences.n: los mios, los vuestros, possessives used as nouns, 'my men, your men'. ferir [los] quiero, 'to strike them I want', the object los, the Moors, restored by Pidal. delant, 'in front'. firme mientre, 'firmly' (mientre, the adverb-maker, = -mente). [a] la çaga, 'at the rear'; the a is Pidal's, though the establishing run is only fairly sure the letter is italic. tengades, present subjunctive, 2nd plural, a polite command. Pidal's note: 'si hubiere peligro bien me podréis socorrer', 'if there be danger, you can well come to my aid': cueta, 'need, distress'; fuere, future subjunctive of seer; podredes, future of poder; huviar, 'to help'.

sentences.t:
Aquí llegó Mynaya Álbar Fáñez:
“Oíd, ya Çid, Canpeador leal[e]!
sentences.l:
Here arrived Mynaya Álbar Fáñez:
“Hear, O Çid, Canpeador loya[l]!
sentences.i: At this Minaya Álvar Fáñez came up: “Hear me, Çid, loyal Campeador!
sentences.n: Aquí, 'here, at this point'. Mynaya, spelt with y as printed. The number 2361b is Pidal's, printed in his margin. ya, 'O' (Arabic yā). leal[e] = leal, 'loyal', with a final e restored by Pidal for the rhyme: the paragogic e, an e added after a final consonant or stressed vowel at the line-end, which the manuscript often leaves unwritten. Pidal prints these restored e's in italics through this tirada (fera[ve], part[e], semejar[e], sera[ve], vagar[e], [estave], buscar[e], matar[e]); the assonance then runs á-e. Note that Minaya ends with !, without ¡, as printed.

sentences.t:
Esta batalla el Criador la fera[ve],
e vos tan dinno que con él avedes part[e].
sentences.l:
This battle the Creator it will-mak[e],
and you so worthy that with him you-have shar[e].
sentences.i: The Creator will win this battle, and you are so worthy that you have your share with him.
sentences.n: Pidal's note: ferave 'hará', con -e paragógica (comp. v. 15), de la cual ponemos aquí una muestra alrededor de la forma Trinidade que aparece en el manuscrito de Pedro Abad — 'ferave, "will make", with a paragogic -e (compare v. 15), of which we give a sample here around the form Trinidade that appears in Per Abbat's manuscript' (v. 2370). ferá is an old future of fazer (= hará); ferá + e gives fera[ve], with a v to bridge the two vowels, the ve Pidal's. Esta batalla … la, the object named first and picked up again by la. dinno = digno, 'worthy'. Pidal's note: con él avedes part, 'tenéis con él favor, acogida' — 'you have favour, welcome with him'. part[e], the e his.

sentences.t:
Mandádno'los ferir de qual part vos semejar[e],
el debdo que [h]a cada uno a conplir sera[ve].
Verlo hemos con Dios e con la vuestra auze.”
sentences.l:
Order-us-them to-strike from which side to-you it-shall-see[m],
the debt that [h]as each one to fulfil will-b[e].
See-it we-shall with God and with the your fortune.”
sentences.i: Order us to strike them from whichever side seems best to you; each man will have to do his duty. We shall see it through with God and with your good fortune.”
sentences.n: Mandádno'los = mandad + nos + los, 'order us … them', imperative 2nd plural with two enclitics; Pidal's apostrophe marks the s of nos lost before los. Pidal's note: 'de la parte que os pareciere', 'from the side that may seem good to you': semejar[e], future subjunctive of semejar, 'seem', the e Pidal's. Pidal's note: 'habrá de cumplirse la obligación que cada uno tiene', 'the duty each one has will have to be fulfilled': debdo, 'debt, duty'; [h]a, 'has', the h his; a conplir sera[ve], 'will be (there) to fulfil', será with the same paragogic ve as fera[ve]. Verlo hemos, the split future: ver + lo + hemos = lo veremos. Pidal's note: auze, 'ventura', 2369, 1523: auze, 'fortune, luck'.

sentences.t: Dixo mio Çid: “ayamos más de vagar[e].”
sentences.l: Said my Çid: “let-us-have more of leisur[e].”
sentences.i: Said my Çid: “Let us take our time.”
sentences.n: Pidal's note: 'tengamos calma', 'esperemos', 'let us keep calm', 'let us wait'. ayamos, present subjunctive of aver, 'let us have'. vagar[e], 'leisure', the noun vagar, with the paragogic e restored by Pidal.

sentences.t:
Afevos el obispo don Jero[me] muy bien armado [estave].
Parávas delant al Campeador siempre con la buen auze:
sentences.l:
Behold-you the bishop don Jero[me] very well armed [is].
He-was-stopping-himself before the Campeador always with the good fortune:
sentences.i: And here is the bishop Don Jerome, very well armed; he planted himself before the Campeador, a man always attended by good fortune:
sentences.n: Afevos, 'behold', the singer pointing his hearers to the scene (a + fe + vos). Jero[me], the me Pidal's. [estave], the whole word Pidal's restoration: most simply está, 'is', with the same paragogic ve as fera[ve], sera[ve]. Parávas = parava + se, 'he stood, set himself', imperfect with enclitic se. delant al Campeador, 'in front of the Campeador'. la buen auze, 'the good fortune' (buen before a feminine noun); Pidal refers this line to his note on auze, 'ventura', at v. 2366. Whose fortune is meant is not said; read with the bishop, the subject of the line.

sentences.i: “Today I sang you the mass of the Holy Trinity. It was for this that I left my own country and came to seek you out: for the longing I had to kill some Moor or other;
sentences.n: dix = dixe, 'I said', strong preterite 1st singular, cut down. Pidal's note: La misa de santa Trinidad, v. 319 — the mass said before battle. Trinidade, with its final e, is the manuscript's own spelling, roman in Pidal: the model for the e's he restores. Por esso, 'for that'. salí, preterite of salir, 'I went out, left'. Pidal's note: 'y vine a buscaros', 'and I came to seek you': vin = vine, cut down, with a bare infinitive, vin vos buscar[e]; buscar[e] here is the infinitive buscar with the paragogic e Pidal restores (not the future subjunctive buscare), as is matar[e], 'to kill'. sabor, 'liking, desire'; de algún moro matar[e], 'of killing some Moor'.

sentences.t:
mi orden e mis manos querría las ondrar,
e a estas feridas yo quiero ir delant.
sentences.l:
my order and my hands I-would-wish them to-honour,
and to these blows I want to-go ahead.
sentences.i: I would do honour to my order and my hands, and I want to lead the way into these blows.
sentences.n: mi orden, 'my order', his holy orders as a bishop. querría, conditional of querer, 'I would wish'; las, picking up orden and manos: 'my order and my hands, I would honour them'. ondrar = honrar. feridas, 'blows' (= heridas), the first clash of the battle. delant, 'ahead, first'.

sentences.t:
Pendón trayo a corças e armas de señal,
si plogiesse a Dios querríalas ensayar,
mio coraçón que pudiesse folgar,
e vos, mio Çid, de mí más vos pagar.
sentences.l:
Pennon I-carry with does and arms of sign,
if it-pleased to God I-would-like-them to-try,
my heart that it-could take-ease,
and you, my Çid, of me more yourself to-be-pleased.
sentences.i: I bear a pennon with does on it, and arms with an emblem; if it pleased God, I should like to try them out, so that my heart might be at ease, and you, my Çid, might be the better pleased with me.
sentences.n: Pidal's note: Verso dudoso. Parece que el obispo lleva en su pendón pintadas unas corzas por señal o blasón; armas de señal son armas con un emblema pintado, para que el caballero fuese conocido en la batalla por los que debían guardarle y seguirle. Téngase en cuenta que en tiempo del Cid estas señales o blasones no eran todavía fijos y hereditarios en las familias — 'a doubtful line. It seems the bishop bears some does painted on his pennon as a sign or blazon; armas de señal are arms with a painted emblem, so that the knight might be known in battle by those who had to guard and follow him. Bear in mind that in the Çid's time these signs were not yet fixed and hereditary in families'. corças, 'does' (corça, the female roe deer); a corças, 'with does', a describing the device; the sense is Pidal's guess. trayo = traigo. plogiesse, imperfect subjunctive of plazer. querríalas = querría + las, conditional with an enclitic object (las, the arms). Pidal's note, printed against v. 2367 but plainly belonging to this line (2376): ensayar 'probar, usar un arma', 2414, 3663. En los versos inmediatos se emplea este verbo con otras dos acepciones diferentes — 'to try, use a weapon … in the lines that follow the verb is used in two other senses' (vv. 2381, 2388). The last two lines hang loosely on querría: 'that my heart might rest, and you be more pleased with me'. folgar = holgar; pagar(se) de, 'to be pleased with'.

sentences.t: Si este amor non feches, yo de vos me quiero quitar.”
sentences.l: If this favour not you-do, I from you myself want to-take-away.”
sentences.i: If you will not do me this favour, I mean to leave your service.”
sentences.n: Pidal's note: 'si no me hacéis este favor, yo me alejaré de vos', 'if you do not do me this favour, I shall go away from you'. amor, here the favour a lord grants his vassal. feches, a reduced form of fazedes, 'you do'. quitarse de, 'to take oneself away from', part from a lord.

sentences.t:
Essora dixo mio Çid: “Lo que vos queredes plazme.
Afé los moros a ojo, idlos ensayar.
Nos d' aquent veremos cómmo lidia el abbat.”
sentences.l:
Then said my Çid: “What you wish pleases-me.
Behold the Moors at eye, go-them to-try.
We from-hither shall-see how fights the abbot.”
sentences.i: Then my Çid said: “What you wish is my pleasure. There are the Moors in plain sight: go and try your hand on them. We will watch from here how the abbot fights.”
sentences.n: Essora, 'then'. plazme = plaze + me, 'pleases me'. Afé, 'behold'; a ojo, 'in sight'. idlos = id + los, 'go … them'. Pidal's note: ensayar, 'acometer', 3318 — 'to attack': the second sense of ensayar. d' aquent, 'from this side, from here' (de + aquent, a cut-down aquende, 'on this side'), printed with a space after the apostrophe. cómmo, 'how'. el abbat, 'the abbot': the Çid gives the armed bishop a cleric's title, and the line has a smile in it. Tirada 116 ends here.

sentences.t:
El obispo don Jero[me] priso a espolonada
e ívalos ferir a cabo del albergada.
sentences.l:
The bishop don Jero[me] took to spur-charge
and was-going-them to-strike at edge of-the encampment.
sentences.i: The bishop Don Jerome led the charge, and rode at them at the edge of the camp.
sentences.n: Tirada 117 (assonance á-a) — the bishop opens the battle; the Çid attacks; he breaks into the Moors' camp (Pidal: El obispo rompe la batalla.—El Cid acomete.—Invade el campamento de los moros). The line-ends run espolonada, albergada, amava, matava, espada: stressed á, then a. Pidal's note: priso a espolonada, 'comenzó el ataque'. La espolonada es la arremetida que unos pocos caballeros, adelantándose a su hueste, hacen contra el enemigo — 'began the attack. The espolonada is the charge that a few knights make against the enemy, riding out ahead of their host' (from espolón, 'spur'). priso, strong preterite of prender, 'took'. Jero[me], the me Pidal's. ívalos ferir = iva + los ferir, 'he went to strike them', imperfect. a cabo del albergada, 'at the end, the edge of the encampment': cabo, 'end'; del for de la before a feminine noun in a- (el albergada, like el espada).

sentences.t:
Por la su ventura e Dios quel amava
a los primeros colpes dos moros matava.
sentences.l:
By the his fortune and God who-him loved
at the first blows two Moors he-was-killing.
sentences.i: By his good fortune, and by the God who loved him, he killed two Moors with his first blows.
sentences.n: la su ventura, article + possessive. quel = que + le, 'who … him': Dios quel amava, 'God, who loved him'. a los primeros colpes, 'at the first blows' (colpe = golpe). matava, imperfect beside preterites: the poem's tenses shift freely.

sentences.t:
El astil a [cr]ebado e metió mano al espada.
Ensayavas el obispo, Dios, qué bien lidiava!
Dos mató con lança e çinco con el espada.
sentences.l:
The shaft he-has [b]roken and put hand to-the sword.
Was-exerting-himself the bishop, God, how well he-was-fighting!
Two he-killed with lance and five with the sword.
sentences.i: His lance-shaft broken, he set his hand to his sword. The bishop gave his all — God, how well he fought! Two he killed with the lance, and five with the sword.
sentences.n: astil, 'shaft' of the lance. a [cr]ebado, 'has broken' (a = ha), the cr Pidal's: crebar = quebrar. metió mano al espada, 'laid hand to the sword', al for a la before espada. Pidal's note: ensayarse, 'esforzarse en la lucha', hacer proezas, 2460; e irónicamente en 2746, 2781 — 'to exert oneself in the fight, do deeds of prowess; and ironically in 2746, 2781': Ensayavas = ensayava + se, the third sense of ensayar in three lines (see vv. 2376, 2381). Dios, qué bien lidiava!, the singer's exclamation, closed with ! and no ¡, as printed.

sentences.t:
Moros son muchos, derredor le çercavan,
dávanle grandes colpes, mas nol falssan las armas.
sentences.l:
Moors are many, around him they-were-surrounding,
they-were-giving-him great blows, but not-to-him pierce the arms.
sentences.i: The Moors were many; they closed in all around him and rained great blows on him, but they cannot break through his armour.
sentences.n: derredor, 'around'. le, 'him', the bishop. dávanle = davan + le, 'they gave him'. nol = non + le, 'not … his', the le standing for whose armour it is: the Moors (subject) do not pierce his arms (las armas, the object). Pidal's note: falssar las armas defensivas, v. 713 — 'to pierce defensive arms': falssan, present of falssar, 'to pierce, break through' armour, sliding into the present among imperfects.

sentences.t:
El que en buen ora nasco los ojos le fincava,
enbraçó el escudo e abaxó el asta,
aguijó a Bavieca, el cavallo que bien anda,
ívalos ferir de coraçón e de alma.
sentences.l:
He who in good hour was-born the eyes on-him was-fixing,
embraced the shield and lowered the lance,
spurred to Bavieca, the horse that well goes,
was-going-them to-strike with heart and with soul.
sentences.i: He who was born in a good hour had his eyes fixed on him; he braced his shield on his arm and lowered his lance, set spurs to Babieca, the horse that runs so well, and rode at them with heart and soul.
sentences.n: el que en buen ora nasco, the Çid. los ojos le fincava, 'was fixing his eyes on him', the bishop; fincar, 'to fix, plant' (= hincar). enbraçó, 'took on the arm' (braço), the shield; abaxó, 'lowered' (x = sh); asta, 'lance' (the shaft for the whole). aguijó a Bavieca, 'spurred Babieca', with the personal a for a named horse. el cavallo que bien anda, 'the horse that goes well'. ívalos ferir, as in v. 2384. de coraçón e de alma, 'with heart and soul'.

sentences.t:
En las azes primeras el Campeador entrava,
abatió a siete e a quatro matava.
sentences.l:
In the ranks first the Campeador was-entering,
threw-down seven and four was-killing.
sentences.i: The Campeador drove into the front ranks; he struck down seven and killed four.
sentences.n: azes, 'ranks, battle lines'. abatió, 'threw down', unhorsed; a siete, a quatro, with the personal a before numbers standing for men. Preterite and imperfect side by side again (abatió … matava).

sentences.t:
Plogo a Dios, aquesta f[o] el arrancada.
Mio Çid con los s[o]s [cade] en alcança;
sentences.l:
It-pleased to God, this w[as] the rout.
My Çid with the h[i]s [falls] in pursuit;
sentences.i: It pleased God that this should be the victory. My Çid and his men are in hot pursuit;
sentences.n: Plogo a Dios, 'it pleased God'. Pidal's note: arrancada, 'victoria': the routing of the enemy. aquesta = esta. f[o] = fue, the o Pidal's. los s[o]s, 'his men', the o his. [cade] en alcança: the whole word cade is Pidal's restoration, the old form of cae, 'falls', present of caer; caer en alcança, 'to fall to the pursuit' (alcança, 'pursuit, overtaking'). The next tirada repeats the phrase as cáenlos en alcaz.

sentences.t:
veriedes [cr]ebar ta[n]tas cuerdas e arrancarse las estacas
e acostarse los tendales, con huebras eran tantas.
sentences.l:
you-would-have-seen [b]reak so-ma[n]y ropes and pull-up-themselves the pegs
and lean-over-themselves the tent-poles, with works they-were so-many.
sentences.i: You would have seen so many tent-ropes snap, and the pegs torn out of the ground, and the tent-poles toppling, so richly worked were they.
sentences.n: veriedes, 'you would have seen', the singer to his hearers. Pidal's note: Para esta descripción comp. v. 1141-42. [cr]ebar, 'to break', the cr Pidal's; ta[n]tas, the n his. arrancarse, acostarse, infinitives with se after veriedes: 'the pegs being pulled up, the tent-poles leaning over'. Pidal's note: con huebras eran tantas, 'tenían muchas labores o adornos'; comp. tendal obrado, 1783 — 'they had much work or adornment; compare the worked tent-pole of v. 1783'. huebras = obras, 'works', here decorative work; literally 'they were so many with work', that is, so much ornamented. The establishing run notes that the h of huebras is damaged in the scan, but the reading is not in doubt.

sentences.t: Los de mio Çid a los de Búcar de las tiendas los sacan.
sentences.l: Those of my Çid to those of Búcar from the tents them they-bring-out.
sentences.i: The Çid's men drive Búcar's men out of their tents.
sentences.n: Los de mio Çid, 'those of my Çid', his men; a los de Búcar, 'those of Búcar', King Búcar's men, the object named first and picked up again by los. sacan, 'they bring out, drive out', present. Tirada 117 ends here; the next tirada opens by repeating the action: Sácanlos de las tiendas.
